blocks.text: Brain Cancer (Brain Tumor)

A brain tumor is an abnormal mass of cells in or around your brain. It can form in your brain or other parts of your central nervous system, like your spine or cranial nerves.

Brain tumors can be cancerous (malignant) or noncancerous (benign). Benign tumors are well-contained and typically grow slowly. Malignant tumors (brain cancer) are much more aggressive and can spread into healthy brain and spinal tissue. Only about one-third of brain tumors are cancerous. But any brain tumor can impact your health if it grows large enough to press on surrounding tissue.

rich.text: Brain tumor symptoms vary depending on the tumor’s location, type, size and growth rate. Benign tumor symptoms are more likely to develop gradually, whereas symptoms from brain cancer may develop more quickly.

blocks.text: Brain tumor symptoms vary depending on the tumor’s location, type, size and growth rate. Benign tumor symptoms are more likely to develop gradually, whereas symptoms from brain cancer may develop more quickly.
Grade 2: The cells are slow-growing and look less like normal cells. The tumor may infiltrate surrounding tissues.

items.answer:
If you have symptoms, a healthcare provider will ask about your medical history and do a neurological exam. If they suspect you may have a brain tumor, an imaging test is usually the next step.

In some cases, providers may discover a brain tumor when doing imaging tests for another reason.

Tests that help confirm a brain tumor diagnosis include:

    MRI or CT scan: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the best imaging test for identifying brain tumors. Computed tomography (CT) is a good alternative if you’re unable to undergo an MRI.
    Biopsy: Providers usually need to get a sample of the tumor for examination under a microscope. This may happen during surgery to remove the tumor or as a separate procedure.
    Biopsy sample testing: Tests can show whether the cells are cancerous and how quickly they’re growing. Other tests can look for DNA changes in the cells. All this information helps determine the best treatment.
items.question: How doctors diagnose this condition?

items:
Researchers have identified more than 150 different brain tumors. Some types include:

    Meningiomas are the most common type of primary brain tumor. They typically develop slowly. They form in the layers of tissue that protect your brain and spinal cord. In rare cases, a meningioma can be malignant.
    Medulloblastoma is fast-growing and forms at the base of your skull. It’s the most common cancerous brain tumor in children.
    Schwannomas develop from Schwann cells, which help with nerve impulses. They’re common benign brain tumors in adults. Acoustic neuromas are the most common type of schwannoma.
    Gliomas form from glial cells. There are four subtypes. Most cases are malignant, but some are benign. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive type of glioma and the most common type of malignant brain tumor in adults.
    Pituitary adenomas form in your pituitary gland, which is at the base of your brain. They’re benign and may release excess hormones.
    Chordomas typically begin at the base of your skull and the bottom part of your spine. They’re slow-growing and mostly benign.
    Craniopharyngiomas arise from a portion of your pituitary gland. They’re difficult tumors to remove because of their location near critical structures deep in your brain.
    Gangliocytomas, gangliomas and anaplastic gangliogliomas are rare tumors that form in neurons (nerve cells).

A brain tumor is an abnormal mass of cells in or around your brain. It can form in your brain or other parts of your central nervous system, like your spine or cranial nerves.

Brain tumors can be cancerous (malignant) or noncancerous (benign). Benign tumors are well-contained and typically grow slowly. Malignant tumors (brain cancer) are much more aggressive and can spread into healthy brain and spinal tissue. Only about one-third of brain tumors are cancerous. But any brain tumor can impact your health if it grows large enough to press on surrounding tissue.

rich.text: Brain tumor symptoms vary depending on the tumor’s location, type, size and growth rate. Benign tumor symptoms are more likely to develop gradually, whereas symptoms from brain cancer may develop more quickly.

items.answer:
If you have symptoms, a healthcare provider will ask about your medical history and do a neurological exam. If they suspect you may have a brain tumor, an imaging test is usually the next step.

In some cases, providers may discover a brain tumor when doing imaging tests for another reason.

Tests that help confirm a brain tumor diagnosis include:

    MRI or CT scan: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the best imaging test for identifying brain tumors. Computed tomography (CT) is a good alternative if you’re unable to undergo an MRI.
    Biopsy: Providers usually need to get a sample of the tumor for examination under a microscope. This may happen during surgery to remove the tumor or as a separate procedure.
    Biopsy sample testing: Tests can show whether the cells are cancerous and how quickly they’re growing. Other tests can look for DNA changes in the cells. All this information helps determine the best treatment.
items.question: How doctors diagnose this condition?

items:
Researchers have identified more than 150 different brain tumors. Some types include:

    Meningiomas are the most common type of primary brain tumor. They typically develop slowly. They form in the layers of tissue that protect your brain and spinal cord. In rare cases, a meningioma can be malignant.
    Medulloblastoma is fast-growing and forms at the base of your skull. It’s the most common cancerous brain tumor in children.
    Schwannomas develop from Schwann cells, which help with nerve impulses. They’re common benign brain tumors in adults. Acoustic neuromas are the most common type of schwannoma.
    Gliomas form from glial cells. There are four subtypes. Most cases are malignant, but some are benign. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive type of glioma and the most common type of malignant brain tumor in adults.
    Pituitary adenomas form in your pituitary gland, which is at the base of your brain. They’re benign and may release excess hormones.
    Chordomas typically begin at the base of your skull and the bottom part of your spine. They’re slow-growing and mostly benign.
    Craniopharyngiomas arise from a portion of your pituitary gland. They’re difficult tumors to remove because of their location near critical structures deep in your brain.
    Gangliocytomas, gangliomas and anaplastic gangliogliomas are rare tumors that form in neurons (nerve cells).

blocks.text: 1. Sage Durvasa's Curse (Krishna and Rukmini)

• The Reason: After marrying Goddess Rukmini, Lord Krishna took her to visit Sage Durvasa to seek his blessings. On their way back, Rukmini became very thirsty and drank water without asking the sage first.
• The Curse: Feeling disrespected, Sage Durvasa cursed Krishna and Rukmini to be separated from each other for 12 years. Rukmini performed intense penance for 12 years to dissolve the curse.
2. Sridama's Curse (Krishna and Radha)

• The Reason: According to the Brahma Vaivarta Purana, Radha became angry and tried to scold Krishna for spending time with another gopi. Krishna's close friend Sridama tried to stop her, leading to a heated argument between them.
• The Curse: Radha cursed Sridama to be born as a demon on Earth, and in return, Sridama cursed Radha to be born as a human and experience a 100-year separation from Krishna.

Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM) represents the most common and aggressive primary malignant brain tumor in adults. Classified as a Grade IV diffusely infiltrating astrocytic glioma under WHO guidelines, GBM is characterized by cellular heterogeneity, microvascular proliferation, and prominent pseudopalisading necrosis.
IDH-wildtype status accounts for ~90% of primary GBM cases and carries a significantly worse overall prognosis compared to IDH-mutant secondary glioblastomas.
